docs.title: Meta-Evolve
docs.text:
Meta-Evolve is a declarative Python library for evaluated evolution over versioned artifacts. Start one bounded job with plain callables, then inspect the complete causal record.

Get started Jobs API reference

docs.title: One complete support job
docs.text:
This is the exact tested source used by the first-evolution guide:

import meta_evolve as meta


SEED = "I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'm looking into it."


def propose(_parent):
    return "I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'll submit a $49 refund today; it should appear in 5–7 business days."


def grade(reply):
    checks = ("#4021" in reply, "$49" in reply and "refund" in reply.lower(), "already refunded" not in reply.lower() and "refund is complete" not in reply.lower())
    return sum(checks) / len(checks)


result = meta.improve(seed=SEED, proposer=propose, evaluator=grade, trials=1)
print(result.best())
RunResult 
uv run python examples/learn/support_response/quickstart.py

I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'll submit a $49 refund today; it should appear in 5–7 business days.

The seed is evaluated as the baseline. The proposer creates a successor, the independent evaluator checks it, and trials bounds the work. The returned Run records the winner, every attempt, lineage, evidence, usage, stop reason, and declarations. Selecting a result never deploys it.

docs.title: Adding an artifact domain
docs.text:
meta.run optimizes whatever you can encode. A domain is one (kind, representation) pair plus the codec that translates between the Python value your proposer and evaluator handle and the durable payload the kernel commits. Adding one takes four small pieces and no change to the library: the coordinator has no branch per domain, which tests/test_four_domain_kernel.py proves by driving number, text, repository, and skill-set runs through one meta.run call site and asserting the same kernel record for all four.

Piece What it is Shipped example Value type what proposers and evaluators see; declares KIND and REPRESENTATION meta.Text Codec encode value → payload, decode payload → value TextCodec Registration Registry.register_artifact_type(codec) built-in codecs skip this Declaration Task(artifact=YourType)

Text is the smallest complete instance and is worth reading first: the value type and its codec are about fifteen lines each. This page builds a second domain — recipe, an ordered list of instruction steps — the same way.

The contracts themselves are canonical elsewhere and are not restated here. ArtifactCodec owns the codec laws, the programming model owns Task, Registry, and meta.run, and the architecture owns what artifacts, kinds, and representations mean.

Every Python block below is one script, run end to end by tests/test_add_a_domain_tutorial.py.

docs.title: 0. Kind and representation
docs.text:
The kind names the schema — what a payload means. The representation names the storage shape that payload is written in. The two are separate because kinds can share a representation: source-tree and skill-set are both utf8-tree-v1, the same portable tree bytes read under different rules. The kind, never the bytes, decides which codec reads a committed payload.

import meta_evolve as meta

print("built-in text domain:", meta.Text.KIND, meta.Text.REPRESENTATION)

docs.title: 1. The value type
docs.text:
Declare KIND and REPRESENTATION as strings on the type; Task(artifact=...) reads exactly those two attributes and nothing else, so a plain class works and no base class is imposed. Subclass whatever Python shape the domain already is — Text is a str, Recipe is a tuple.

Rules that decide whether a value is one of these belong here, in the constructor. Rules about whether a value is any good belong to the evaluator.

from typing import ClassVar


class Recipe(tuple):
    """An ordered sequence of instruction steps."""

    KIND: ClassVar[str] = "recipe"
    REPRESENTATION: ClassVar[str] = "json-steps-v1"

    __slots__ = ()

    def __new__(cls, steps=()):
        steps = tuple(steps)
        if not all(isinstance(step, str) and step.strip() for step in steps):
            raise ValueError("every recipe step must be non-blank text")
        return super().__new__(cls, steps)

docs.title: 2. The codec
docs.text:
encode and decode must be pure, deterministic, and free of I/O, and decode is the only validation entry point — a codec has no separate validate. Return any payload freeze accepts: None, bool, int, finite float, str, lists and tuples of those, and string-keyed mappings of those. Artifact freezes what you return and derives the content digest from it, so codecs never mint or check identity.

Refuse a value that is not yours by raising TypeError or ValueError. Those two are the rejection signal and nothing else is: encode is reached by every proposed candidate as well as by the seed, so a refusal there fails that one trial as a typed InvalidOutput and the run continues, while any other exception is treated as a bug in the codec and propagates.

class RecipeCodec:
    """Translates ``Recipe`` values to and from their durable payload."""

    kind = Recipe.KIND
    representation = Recipe.REPRESENTATION
    interfaces = ("ordered-steps/v1",)

    def encode(self, value):
        if not isinstance(value, Recipe):
            raise TypeError("recipe tasks require a Recipe value")
        return tuple(value)

    def decode(self, payload):
        return Recipe(payload)

interfaces names what a consumer may rely on, independently of the kind, so a later artifact carrying the same structure can declare the same interface and reuse its consumers. Leave it () when nothing consumes the domain structurally yet. kind, representation, and every interface name are identity declarations: each must be non-empty and have no outer whitespace. Registration rejects invalid declarations rather than trimming them.

docs.title: 3. Register the codec
docs.text:
registry = meta.Registry()
registry.register_artifact_type(RecipeCodec())
print("declared interfaces:", registry.artifact_interfaces("recipe", "json-steps-v1"))

Registration is keyed by (kind, representation). The six built-in keys are not overridable — changing the decode of an old key would change the meaning of every artifact already committed under it — so a different behavior needs a different key. A new representation of a built-in kind is a different key and registers normally.

docs.title: 4. Declare it on the task and run
docs.text:
Pass the registry to meta.run and name the value type on the task. From here nothing is domain-specific: the proposer receives decoded values and returns one, the evaluator scores one, and search, budgets, lineage, and experience behave exactly as they do for integers.

def add_step(parent, context):
    return Recipe((*parent, f"step {len(parent) + 1}"))


def score(candidate):
    return {"score": float(len(candidate))}


experiment = meta.Experiment(
    task=meta.Task(
        evaluator=score,
        artifact=Recipe,
        budget=meta.Budget(evaluations=4, trials=3),
    ),
    seed=Recipe(("preheat the oven",)),
    proposer=add_step,
    search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=3),
    registry=registry,
)
result = meta.run(experiment)

best = result.best()
print("committed as:", best.kind, best.representation)
print("decoded type:", type(best.value).__name__)
print("best value:", tuple(best.value))
print("primary score:", result.summary().primary_score)

built-in text domain: text utf8-text-v1
declared interfaces: ('ordered-steps/v1',)
committed as: recipe json-steps-v1
decoded type: Recipe
best value: ('preheat the oven', 'step 2', 'step 3', 'step 4')
primary score: 4.0

That is the whole domain. The script imports meta_evolve and the standard library, and touches no library file.

docs.title: 5. Check the codec against the published suite
docs.text:
meta_evolve.conformance.ArtifactCodecTests checks both round trips, repeated-call stability within one process, common file/socket entry points, TypeError/ValueError rejection of foreign values and of malformed payloads (rejected_payloads — decode is validation), decoding through the kernel's CodecIndex, and — for values declared in mutable_values — that a decoded value is independent of the one you encoded. No law compares values with ==: observations go through value_state, whose default knows exact canonical and kernel types only. Recipe subclasses tuple, so its suite overrides value_state with tuple(value) — an observation the codec has no hand in. The I/O patches are tripwires, not proof of arbitrary purity, and repeated calls do not prove cross-process reproducibility. Subclass the suite and override five fixtures (plus value_state for your own value types and mutate if any value is mutable); the published-conformance section of the extensions guide has the snippet and the install extra. RecipeCodec above is checked that way in this tutorial's own test.

Every component family a registered domain composes with — codecs, repository-editing proposers, evaluators, search programs, context policies, workspaces, sandboxes, and typed mutation surfaces — has a published subclassable suite; see meta_evolve.conformance for what each deliberately leaves unchecked.

docs.title: What a registered domain does not get yet
docs.text: • Restart-resumable execution. mode="durable-local" fails closed with CapabilityError for any task whose (kind, representation) is not one of the six built-in keys. A registered codec is a live object rather than registered source, so it carries no manifest and a resumed run could not verify that the code rebuilding a payload is the code that wrote it. Custom domains are local mode in Milestone 7. They may still use durable storage: after reopening the storage and reconstructing the registry, inspect one through meta.Run(run_id, storage, registry=registry). This is decoding only, not resume or execution authority; command-line inspection remains built-in-only.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Meta-Evolve evaluates proposed successors to immutable, versioned artifacts. The domain meaning does not depend on an artifact kind, model provider, search preset, evaluator implementation, or storage backend.

Task -> Seed -> Proposal -> Successor -> Evaluation -> Search decision
                      \-> typed failure

The public callable path hides kernel ceremony. Durable records retain the facts needed for lineage, accounting, inspection, comparison, and replay.

docs.title: Architectural layers
docs.text:
Public API       improve, Task, artifacts, Session, run/resume, result queries
Application      normalization, coordination, comparison, replay
Domain           immutable identities, outcomes, evidence, budgets
Ports            proposer, evaluator, experience, workspace, storage
Adapters         callables, SDK agents, subprocesses, files, SQLite

Dependencies point inward. Adapters translate external systems at the edge; the coordinator never branches on a provider, artifact type, evaluator, policy, or infrastructure implementation.

docs.title: Identities and lineage
docs.text:
Content identity and occurrence identity are distinct. Equal artifact bytes may appear in different causal positions and therefore retain different occurrence IDs and parent links. Task, run, proposal, trial, evaluation, evidence, decision, and component identities are not collapsed for storage convenience.

Every successor names its parents. Every decision-relevant observation is recorded at a logical time. Durable state is a projection of immutable records, not a mutable branch, workspace, cache, or provider conversation.

docs.title: Authority boundaries
docs.text: Candidate-controlled fields contain only proposed artifact content and declared derivation. Experiment-controlled fields include tasks, evaluators, data splits, seeds, environments, and budgets. Governance controls permissions, admission, visibility, and promotion.

docs.title: Proposal and promotion are separate
docs.text: Search may select a best measured artifact. That selection grants no production authority. A candidate cannot widen its budget, alter hidden evaluation, erase failures, change permissions, or promote itself. Future typed mutation surfaces must preserve this invariant; see the M8 design.

docs.title: Evaluation and failures
docs.text: Evaluation is independent of candidate claims and carries measurements, uncertainty, evidence, environment identity, and exact usage. Invalid output, proposer failure, evaluator failure, timeout, exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure remain distinct. An outcome without a valid measurement is non-rankable.

docs.title: Budgets and randomness
docs.text: The coordinator owns accounting. Seed evaluation and successor work charge the declared dimensions exactly; experience access has separate bounds. Named random streams and recorded decisions make deterministic local trajectories replayable. External provider calls are reproducible only to the recorded transcript and declarations, not guaranteed to regenerate byte-identical output.

docs.title: Experience
docs.text: Experience is explicit and off by default. Pushed context is policy-selected, bounded, and committed before a proposal. Pulled experience is capability- bounded and audited. Declared derivation may cite only authorized, strictly prior observations in their recorded order.

docs.title: Workspaces and external execution
docs.text:
Repository proposers receive a private mutable workspace from an immutable artifact. Capture creates a new immutable occurrence; cleanup precedes commitment. Evaluators materialize candidates in fresh workspaces and own their commands, environments, hidden graders, and failure translation.

WorkspaceProvider.capture() reserves ValueError for unrepresentable content; ownership, availability, and provider faults become infrastructure failures. WorkspaceProposer scrubs bytecode without following symlinks, captures the complete tree, and always disposes it. An unchanged capture succeeds as a new occurrence; harness-v2 deliberately applies a different no-op rule.

docs.title: Durability and replay
docs.text:
Artifacts and append-only transitions are durable truth. SQLite and filesystem stores preserve committed facts; caches and worker liveness do not. Reopen is a read-only projection, and a read-only storage handle observes live WAL commits with no write, migration, or execution authority. Resume first verifies component manifests and the recovery frontier, then performs only missing logical work. Replay never reruns a proposer, evaluator, context selector, or provider. Run.inspect() derives one immutable aggregate from one replay. Session fixes authority and budget; each step advances the classified frontier to ready or stopped without asking search twice. Lifecycle means Stop, rankability means successful evaluation, and bootstrap remains a trial.

Safe presentation reads frozen payloads into bounded inert records; decoded values are never inspected and canonical attachments remain exact. The browser keeps storage on one thread and artifact routes within one snapshot.

docs.title: Replaceability
docs.text: An independently testable port is introduced only when a current acceptance test needs a second implementation. Every extension seam — codecs, repository proposers, evaluators, search programs, context policies, workspaces, sandboxes, and typed mutation surfaces — has a published conformance suite; store adapters keep an internal contract under tests/. Each suite remains explicit about the laws it does not check.

docs.title: Improve
docs.text: improve() is declaration sugar with no independent durable identity or execution semantics. It constructs Task, bounded Greedy, and Experiment values and enters the ordinary local run() path. Its storage argument may persist local history, but does not imply durable-local reconstruction or resumability.

docs.title: Experiment
docs.text: Experiment is an immutable declaration value, not a new durable record or serialization identity. Positional typed declarations and the source-compatible keyword run() form normalize before validation and enter the same execution path. Storage, mode, and the narrowing call-level budget remain execution overlays. Equality is dataclass equality over the eight fields; it does not promise structural equality for live proposer or registry objects.

docs.title: Functional search
docs.text: @search is a dependency-free adapter over the ordinary SearchProgram boundary, not a second coordinator path. Its callback chooses one opaque seed or incumbent occurrence handle, or stops with a validated reason. A private shared lowerer applies the same envelope and authorized unit trial construction as Greedy; the two retain distinct truthful policy and run identities. Complete immutable decorator configuration flows into SearchSpec and run identity. Durable-local reconstruction remains explicit registration through the existing policy-factory extension. Multiple parents, archives, and population-shaped actions stay on SearchProgram.next().

docs.title: Programming harnesses
docs.text:
Harness is the built-in agent-harness domain using harness-v2. It is plain frozen data containing planner text and an immutable context-policy mapping. The payload contains exactly those two fields and no schema or declaration blocks.

Artifact codecs may structurally expose validate_successor(parents, candidate). Proposal completion invokes it after candidate encoding and before artifact creation. Codecs without the hook retain their behavior. This generic boundary is core-owned. Harness-v2 requires exactly one parent and rejects malformed and no-op successors as InvalidOutput.

Harness search evaluates development episodes only. Held-out episodes run once for the unchanged baseline and once for the selected harness as seed-only Greedy(max_trials=0) runs. Strict comparison requires equal evaluator, artifact, objective, budget, proposer, search, randomness, context, experience, and environment. It reports promotion eligibility but owns no promotion or deployment authority.

Repository episode records belong to the deterministic harness example, their only consumer. That evaluator launches fresh isolated inner runs and records complete captured attempts. Resume guarantees begin at a committed outer evaluation; uncommitted inner work may repeat.

docs.title: Nested improvement loops
docs.text:
PolicyArtifact is the built-in search-policy domain using policy-manifest-v1. Its only mutable values are parent selection (seed or incumbent) and a non-negative voluntary trial limit. Fixed schema-owned names, component declarations, interfaces, allowed domains, tasks, seeds, proposers, evaluators, environments, budgets, split membership, caching, aggregation, and promotion remain outside candidate authority.

CandidatePolicy is the trusted candidate-policy@1 interpreter registered through the ordinary policy registry. Its canonical artifact payload is the search configuration and therefore part of the existing RunId; durable-local reconstruction and resume require no coordinator branch.

Policy episodes are user-owned composition around ordinary runs. Each isolated inner run retains its own events, lineage, evidence, failures, usage, RunId, and evaluator-owned storage location. The existing content-addressed RunId is the sole cache identity. Development may reopen an exact completed run or resume a compatible incomplete durable run. Held-out execution always starts in a new empty namespace. Aggregates are recomputed from outcomes rather than cached separately.

Any failed, incomplete, or missing episode makes an evaluation non-rankable while preserving partial outcomes. Inner trial/evaluation counts remain inner; only token and elapsed usage rolls into an enclosing evaluation. Separate seed-only held-out outer runs compare the baseline and selected candidate under equal external controls. Comparison reports promotion eligibility without granting promotion authority. See the policy-evolution guide.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
• Artifacts are immutable; equal content does not collapse causal occurrences.
  • Parent lineage, component identity, randomness, evidence, and usage are explicit.
  • Candidates cannot control evaluation, budgets, permissions, or promotion.
  • Failures without valid measurements are never ranked as low scores.
  • Replay projects committed facts without external execution.
  • Replaceable components enter through ports, never coordinator special cases.

docs.title: How Meta-Evolve compares
docs.text:
This page answers a question new readers ask first: AlphaEvolve, GEPA's optimize_anything, and Meta-Evolve all run "propose, evaluate, keep the better one" loops — so what is actually different, and when would you pick each?

Claims about external systems belong to the linked first-party materials. Nothing here implies Meta-Evolve has reproduced their results; consult those sources for current availability and product details.

docs.title: One sentence each
docs.text:
• AlphaEvolve is Google DeepMind's hosted discovery service: you bring a problem and an automated evaluator, Google brings the coding agent, the search, and the compute. It is not part of this open-source library.
  • GEPA's optimize_anything is an open-source (MIT) optimizer: a strong reflective-mutation algorithm with Pareto selection, packaged behind a deliberately tiny API — a seed plus an evaluator.
  • Meta-Evolve is an open kernel: a programming model for building your own evaluated improvement loop out of replaceable parts, where every run leaves a durable, replayable, budget-exact record.

All three run the same loop shape. They sell different layers of it:

                 AlphaEvolve   optimize_anything   Meta-Evolve
the results      product       headline            not yet demonstrated
the algorithm    internal      product             simple presets
the loop itself  internal      internal            product

AlphaEvolve's product is the results (you rent the whole system). GEPA's product is the algorithm (the loop is fixed; you feed it). Meta-Evolve's product is the loop itself (you program it; the kernel guarantees the record).

docs.title: What "control" means here, concretely
docs.text:
Many frameworks are "flexible" through configuration flags. Meta-Evolve is different in a specific way: the loop is programmed, not configured. Each stage — proposer, evaluator, search program, context policy, artifact codec, workspace, storage — is a seam with a published contract and a conformance suite. You swap implementations, not flags.

The practical payoff is ablation. Because a component can be replaced without touching anything else, you can run the identical task several ways under equal budgets and compare the records:

task = meta.Task(evaluator=score_candidate)

for context in (meta.policies.NoMemory(), meta.policies.AncestorsOnly(), meta.policies.PullAccess()):
    experiment = meta.Experiment(
        task=task,
        seed=seed,
        proposer=improve,
        search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=20),
        context=context,
    )
    result = meta.run(experiment)
    print(type(context).__name__, result.best(), result.experience_usage())

That is a controlled experiment on the loop's own memory policy: same task, same proposer, same budget, one variable changed. The experience A/B example runs exactly this comparison. The same move works for search (Greedy vs BestOfN vs Population — see the policy comparison) and for proposers.

A monolithic optimizer cannot ablate itself this way. In optimize_anything, reflection and Pareto selection live inside the loop; there is no seam at which to remove or replace one of them while holding the rest fixed. That is not a defect — it is the price of a two-argument API — but it means questions like "did the memory help?" or "was it the selection rule or the mutation?" are answerable in Meta-Evolve and not from inside a sealed loop.

docs.title: Control is half; the record is the other half
docs.text:
Swappable parts alone would just be do-it-yourself. The second half is that whatever you plug in, the kernel still enforces the same invariants:

  • Independent evaluation. The evaluator measures the candidate outside the proposer's authority. A candidate cannot grade itself, widen its own budget, erase failures, or promote itself (architecture: authority boundaries).
  • Exact budgets. Seed evaluation, successor attempts, and experience access charge declared budget dimensions exactly, so "equal budget" comparisons are equal by construction, not by convention.
  • Lineage. Every successor names its parents; every decision-relevant observation is recorded at a logical time. run.lineage() is the exact causal chain, and proposers can declare which prior records they used through derived_from.
  • Replay. A durable run can be reopened and replayed to a byte-identical event stream (persistence/recovery example). Stated precisely: replay reproduces the recorded run exactly; it does not re-execute a stochastic model. That is what a reviewer needs to check a claim, and it is the part most optimizer libraries do not attempt.

Text-only optimizers also collapse artifact structure into strings: a candidate is well-formed only if the evaluator happens to reject malformed text at scoring time. Meta-Evolve artifacts are typed — source trees take exact-file patches through private workspaces, skill sets and harnesses have declared interfaces — and successors are validated against their parent before commit (add a domain).

docs.title: What the others do better
docs.text:
Honesty in both directions:

  • Call-site simplicity. optimize_anything is a seed and an evaluator. Meta-Evolve's smallest path is improve(): seed, proposer, evaluator, and a trial bound. That is still more ceremony than a seed-plus-evaluator optimizer. For "make this prompt better this afternoon," the smaller API is simply the better tool, and the determinism ceremony here is friction with no payoff.
  • A strong proposer out of the box. GEPA ships state-of-the-art reflective mutation; AlphaEvolve ships a frontier coding agent. Meta-Evolve deliberately bundles no model — the shipped presets are simple, and the intelligence is whatever you connect at the proposer seam.
  • Demonstrated results. AlphaEvolve and GEPA lead with headline numbers. Meta-Evolve's examples are deterministic teaching loops; it has not yet produced a live optimization result of its own. Its claims are about the loop's guarantees, not about optimization performance.

docs.title: Choosing in practice
docs.text:
• Improving one prompt or config quickly, cheap evaluations, nobody will audit the run → optimize_anything.
  • Enterprise code optimization with managed compute and no infrastructure appetite → AlphaEvolve on Google Cloud.
  • Controlled experiments on the loop itself (memory, search, proposer ablations), expensive or noisy evaluations where crash recovery and exact accounting matter, bi-level autoresearch setups, or any run whose record must justify a promotion decision → Meta-Evolve.

docs.title: Using them together
docs.text:
These tools compose rather than compete. GEPA-style reflective mutation is, from Meta-Evolve's point of view, a proposer: a callable that reads the parent and prior evidence and returns a ProposalResult (SDK integration). Pareto-frontier retention is a search program behind the same contract as Greedy and Population (extensions). Hosted that way, the optimizer keeps its intelligence and the kernel adds lineage, budgets, and replay.

The same seams make Meta-Evolve usable as a neutral harness for comparing optimizers under exactly equal budgets on identical records — a comparison no single optimizer can run on itself from the inside. Adapter compatibility with existing frameworks is the stated preference over duplicating their APIs; see OpenEvolve in the references.

docs.text:
Status: Experimental/live-only. Meta-Evolve ships no provider client or credentialed launcher. Use the shipped SDK-integration guide to wrap your own client as a callable or structural proposer.

The current examples are credential-free and deterministic. Their injection points can be used by an opt-in maintainer driver:

Exercise Injection point Maximum wrapper calls Repository proposal examples/agents/code_repair 1 Experience A/B examples/agents/experience_ab 4 Held-out skill evolution examples/domains/skill_evolution 6

The ceiling is a declaration for a driver, not permission to spend. The driver must identify its wrapper and behavior-affecting configuration, authenticate outside Meta-Evolve, require explicit opt-in, and preserve SDK-specific tools, permissions, timeouts, and telemetry at the edge.

Only shared Meta-Evolve facts are comparable: task, seed, evaluator, effective budget, search declaration, durable usage, failures, lineage, and audited experience. A provider or infrastructure failure, timeout, invalid candidate, missing derivation, or grader failure carries no score and must never be converted to zero.

There is no official provider capture pending. A user may perform one authorized run with their own wrapper. Any published capture must name the wrapper declaration and retain ties, failures, and regressions honestly. CI uses deterministic fixtures and performs no credentialed execution.

docs.text: Status: Shipped. This is the canonical contract for the public API available from the current package. The generated API reference owns signatures and parameter details; the guides own task-oriented usage. The concise project-status page separates shipped, experimental, and design-only work and links the milestone records.

docs.title: Public execution model
docs.text:
improve() is the small author path: it accepts a seed, proposer, evaluator, and trial bound and returns a Run. The tested support-response program and first-result explanation live in Your first evolution, their authoritative teaching home.

The expanded declaration separates a Task—what better means and what work is allowed—from an Experiment— the seed, proposer, search policy, context, experience, and random seed. The precise lowering from improve() to Task, Experiment, and run() is owned by Evaluated evolution.

For 1.x compatibility, the source-compatible declaration-keyword spelling lowers through the same Experiment; new author material uses the typed form. The compatibility call remains:

meta.run(task=..., seed=..., proposer=..., search=...)

Experiment owns the eight declaration fields and defaults. Storage, mode, and a narrowing call-level budget are execution overlays on run(), never experiment fields.

The returned Run is both the result and the query surface for aggregate inspection, trials, lineage, evidence, usage, failures, summaries, and comparisons.

Safe frozen-payload presentation, direct-parent diff rules, and exact current canonical-payload-v1 bytes are specified by the browser guide.

run() exhausts the same synchronous Session available for paced execution. Session fixes the experiment, effective budget, components, and authority at start. Each step() commits one decision or completes one owed by recovery, then returns its immutable DecisionView; it accepts no injected decision. Bootstrap is complete before Session.start() returns and is not a policy step.

Durable storage has two independent axes: is_durable means committed facts live on durable media, while is_read_only means this handle has no commit or execution authority. Storage.durable(path) is durable and writable; Storage.read_only(path) is durable and read-only. Storage.run_version(id) returns the maximum committed event sequence, or 0 when that well-formed id has no events. The latter is a polling result, not authoritative run loading: opening a required missing run still raises RunNotFound.

docs.title: Authority and failure boundary
docs.text:
Candidates may propose artifact content. They cannot change the evaluator, effective budget, permissions, hidden data, audit history, or promotion rule. Invalid output, proposer/evaluator failure, timeout, exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure remain typed, inspectable outcomes. A failure with no valid measurement is never ranked as a low score.

Harness candidates receive a second, trusted check after codec encoding and before artifact creation. The built-in harness-v2 codec requires exactly one parent and rejects malformed or no-op transitions as InvalidOutput. Harness content has no authority declarations; evaluator, budget, and governance authority remain in Task and Experiment.

@meta.search(max_trials=20)

docs.title: Research and Systems References
docs.text:
This is a working map of neighboring ideas. Meta-Evolve should implement, compose, and compare these approaches rather than rename one of them as a universal solution. For a plain-language comparison with AlphaEvolve and GEPA's optimize_anything, see How Meta-Evolve compares.

Claims about capabilities in these papers belong to the cited systems. Their inclusion here does not mean Meta-Evolve has reproduced their results.

docs.title: Experience Graphs / Trellis
docs.text:
Experience Graphs: The Data Foundation for Self-Improving Agents treats the causal state produced by long-horizon search—attempts, executable artifacts, prompts, tool outputs, rewards, siblings, search statistics, and lineage—as governed database state.

Important implications for Meta-Evolve:

  • stateless agents can recover and collaborate through durable shared experience;
  • online search, causal traversal, semantic reuse, temporal reconstruction, observability, and training views operate over one logical model;
  • the system must preserve the state observed when a decision was made, not only final mutated search statistics;
  • experience retrieval is a policy with an exploration-versus-anchoring tradeoff;
  • derived skills and training views inherit provenance and access constraints.

The paper reports preliminary domain-specific results for cross-session reuse in kernel optimization, including faster early convergence and fewer buggy nodes, while aggressive reuse reduced strategy diversity and missed the best final candidate. This motivates controlled context-policy experiments rather than a general claim that more memory always improves search.

Trellis overlaps with Meta-Evolve's data plane, not its entire product scope. Meta-Evolve focuses additionally on programmable harness and search abstractions, execution adapters, contributed agents/evaluators/compute, verification, and federation.

docs.title: DSPy
docs.text:
DSPy provides a declarative programming model for modular LM programs and optimizers that compile prompts and demonstrations against metrics.

Meta-Evolve should integrate DSPy in both directions:

  • wrap a DSPy program as a versioned harness component;
  • use a DSPy optimizer for an inner prompt/program compilation loop;
  • expose Meta-Evolve examples and evaluators as DSPy-compatible data and metrics;
  • capture compiled programs as immutable artifacts;
  • let an outer Meta-Evolve policy compare DSPy with other optimizers.

The boundary is: DSPy programs LM pipelines; Meta-Evolve programs and evolves populations of executable systems, including DSPy pipelines.

docs.title: GEPA
docs.text: GEPA uses reflective textual mutation and Pareto selection to optimize LM components from task feedback. It is a reference for TextArtifact mutation, evidence-aware reflection, and Pareto retention.

docs.title: Feedback Descent
docs.text: Feedback Descent motivates structured comparison feedback followed by feedback-derived prompt edits. The research lab isolates that mechanism without claiming to reproduce its results.

docs.title: AutoData
docs.text: AutoData motivates evolving data-generation recipes with solver-based quality signals. The local lab's same-model/different-context restricted/informed setup is explicitly a teaching simplification and confounder.

docs.title: EvoSkill
docs.text: EvoSkill motivates failure-driven discovery, consolidation, and held-out selection of reusable skills. Meta-Evolve should express this as evolution of SkillArtifact and SkillSetArtifact objects rather than a special memory subsystem.

docs.title: Meta-Harness
docs.text:
Meta-Harness moves optimization beyond prompts to the source code and control logic surrounding a fixed model. It motivates harness artifacts, explicit editable data, full execution history, and external authority boundaries.

Its agentic proposer can selectively inspect the source, scores, and execution traces of prior candidates through a filesystem instead of receiving only compressed feedback. Meta-Evolve should preserve this agent-directed exploration as a scoped ExperienceReader capability alongside policy-pushed context. A read-only filesystem projection can provide compatibility for coding agents, while structured graph tools add causal traversal, logical-time queries, provenance, and governance.

docs.title: Shepherd
docs.text:
Shepherd is a runtime substrate that records an agent's model actions, tool calls, and environment changes as a reversible, forkable execution trace. Its unit of control is an execution in progress; Meta-Evolve's unit of evolution is an immutable artifact evaluated between trials. The two models are therefore adjacent rather than interchangeable.

A useful composition would keep Meta-Evolve in charge of tasks, search, budgets, independent evaluation, lineage, and promotion while a user-owned Shepherd-backed proposer supplies isolated execution, retained workspace output, and trace-level evidence. Any such integration should begin as an external adapter experiment: the captured artifact remains durable truth, trace references are supporting evidence, and restored or forked execution must not bypass trial or usage accounting. Shepherd's visual-artifact notebooks are also a useful teaching reference for deterministic-first examples, optional live runs, and progressive disclosure of execution internals.

docs.title: Asari inference-stack optimization
docs.text:
Asari's inference-optimization report describes many agents improving a pinned vLLM serving stack through a discover/build, evaluate, verify, and self-improve loop. It reports changes across kernels, schedulers, load balancing, and configuration, using hierarchical performance benchmarks, measurement-noise controls, and token-distribution correctness checks.

A bounded Meta-Evolve version maps cleanly onto current seams:

  • a small SourceTree overlay holds candidate kernel and configuration edits;
  • a user-owned SDK proposer investigates and changes that overlay;
  • a custom evaluator builds it against an evaluator-owned base, verifies model behavior, and returns performance metrics, uncertainty, evidence, and usage;
  • context or audited experience exposes earlier profiler and failure evidence;
  • search retains alternatives while lineage records which evidence informed each change; and
  • an external decision, never the candidate, owns production promotion.

The shipped CommandEvaluator is only a binary, single-metric exit-code adapter, so a trustworthy experiment needs a domain evaluator that parses repeated benchmark samples. A local sequential precursor is feasible, but a whole-stack implementation also needs typed mutation surfaces and portable episodes from M8 and M9, plus trusted parallel GPU workers from M11. Cross-run knowledge transfer must be introduced explicitly rather than silently widening M3's same-run experience boundary.

Meta-Evolve does not reproduce Asari's results. The scoped future work is tracked in issue #118: start with one kernel on one trusted GPU, preserve null and negative results, and defer many-agent whole-stack optimization until its dependencies ship.

docs.title: AIDE²
docs.text: Weco's AIDE² report describes a bi-level experiment in which an outer autoresearch loop rewrites an inner research agent, evaluates each rewrite across heterogeneous tasks under a fixed cost, and selects using private scores. Its reported empirical claims belong to that system. Meta-Evolve's autoresearch teaching example demonstrates only the small nested-run, budget, evidence, and split boundaries; it is not a reproduction or evidence of recursive self-improvement.

docs.title: AlphaEvolve
docs.text: AlphaEvolve demonstrates coding-agent-driven evolutionary search for algorithmic and scientific problems. It is a reference for program artifacts, evaluator-guided evolution, and populations of executable candidates.

docs.title: FunSearch
docs.text: FunSearch combines LLM-generated programs with automated evaluation and evolutionary selection for mathematical discovery. It illustrates why executable artifacts and objective evaluators are powerful while also showing that the evaluator and representation bound the discovery process.

docs.title: OpenEvolve
docs.text: OpenEvolve is an open evolutionary coding-agent framework and useful implementation reference for program databases, evaluation, and search loops. Meta-Evolve should seek adapter compatibility where practical rather than duplicate APIs without benefit.

docs.title: EvoX
docs.text: EvoX motivates treating both solutions and the search strategy as evolving artifacts. This corresponds to nested task evaluation of PolicyArtifact and SearchProgram candidates.

docs.title: Group-Evolving Agents
docs.text: Group-Evolving Agents studies evolution at the level of composite agent groups and shared experience. It is relevant to TopologyArtifact, performance-novelty selection, and group-level mutation.

docs.title: Agent0 and Dr. Zero
docs.text: Agent0 and Dr. Zero explore proposer-solver co-evolution and self-generated curricula under verifiable rewards. They motivate explicit curriculum, checkpoint, training-job, and evaluator artifacts with separate validation boundaries.

docs.title: AERO
docs.text: AERO couples self-questioning, answering, criticism, and iterative model updates. It is relevant to synthetic-experience artifacts and external training loops consuming experience-graph views.

docs.title: CORAL
docs.text: CORAL is relevant to parallel coding agents, evaluated repository successors, shared knowledge, islands, and migration. In Meta-Evolve this becomes one GitTreeArtifact task configuration rather than the universal runtime model.

docs.title: Quality diversity and island models
docs.text: Quality-diversity methods, novelty search, MAP-Elites, Pareto archives, and island models are important baselines for maintaining heterogeneous strategies and avoiding premature convergence. They should be implemented as replaceable population and migration policies.

docs.title: MemGPT
docs.text: MemGPT frames agent memory as a hierarchy that moves information between limited context and external storage. Meta-Evolve's ContextPolicy operates at this transport boundary, while the experience graph defines durable causal search state beneath it.

docs.title: Graphiti and structured memory
docs.text: Graphiti is relevant to temporal knowledge graphs and dynamic synthesis of agent memory. Meta-Evolve additionally needs executable artifacts, objective rewards, search-policy state, training views, and causal sibling/path queries.

docs.title: Event sourcing and content addressing
docs.text:
Event sourcing, temporal databases, MVCC/change-data capture, content-addressed storage, reproducible build systems, and scientific provenance systems provide established foundations for immutable facts, current projections, time travel, lineage, deduplication, and audit.

Meta-Evolve should reuse conventional database and storage systems until its measured workload demonstrates a need for specialized physical design.

docs.title: Research questions for Meta-Evolve
docs.text:
• When does heterogeneous agent diversity improve compute-normalized progress?
  • Which context policies accelerate reuse without suppressing novelty?
  • Which topologies and migration policies avoid premature convergence?
  • How should compute be allocated among exploration, exploitation, repair, synthesis, and replication?
  • Which graph features predict the value of expanding or abandoning a branch?
  • How do skills and discoveries transfer across models, harnesses, tasks, and domains?
  • Which consistency guarantees are sufficient for concurrent search?
  • How should access changes and retractions propagate into derived skills, datasets, and checkpoints?
  • Can learned or evolved search policies generalize to held-out task distributions?
  • When do nested improvement loops plateau, destabilize, or exploit evaluators?
  • What evidence and replication policies predict real scientific validity?

docs.title: SealQA research labs
docs.text:
Status: Experimental/live-only. These are teaching mechanisms, not paper reproductions or an official SealQA evaluation.

The four chapters cover Feedback Descent, AutoData, a historical harness precursor, and EvoSkill. Their implementations live in examples/research/sealqa_labs/ and share one explicit SessionRunner boundary. Meta-Evolve supplies orchestration and deterministic test runners; you supply any live SDK wrapper.

docs.title: Fixed controls
docs.text:
Fixture questions, evaluator answers, schemas, session limits, and mutation allowlists stay outside candidate authority. Solver views contain only public document identifiers, titles, dates, and text. A wrapper owns authentication, structured decoding, tools, permissions, model configuration, and provider telemetry.

Malformed output, timeout, exhaustion, SDK failure, and protected-control edits are typed and unrankable. Deterministic graders alone produce rankable metrics. Every session retains its label, decoded value or failure, evidence, usage, and experience counters.

docs.title: Run with your own wrapper
docs.text:
Create an opt-in driver outside the shipped examples, implement build_agent(request), and pass it to UserSdkSessionRunner. Review the maximum call count, permissions, and spending limit before enabling live work.

No official provider capture is pending. Published captures must identify the wrapper declaration and preserve ties, failures, null results, and regressions.

docs.title: Keep authority where it belongs
docs.text: A proposer can claim anything — a confident claim is not a measurement. Meta-Evolve survives unreliable proposers because every field in a run has exactly one owner. Your first evolution demonstrates the separation; this page names it.

docs.title: Three fields, three owners
docs.text:
A trial's record splits into three kinds of fields:

  • Candidate-controlled — the proposed artifact content and its declared citations. Everything a proposer decides, and nothing else.
  • Experiment-controlled — the task, evaluator, hidden data, environment, seeds, and budgets. The evaluator scores independently; a proposer's claim about its own quality never moves a metric.
  • Governance-controlled — permissions, admission, visibility, and promotion. These live outside the run entirely.
candidate            experiment             governance
─────────            ──────────             ──────────
artifact content     evaluator + data       permissions
declared citations   budgets + seeds        visibility
                     environments           promotion

A candidate cannot read or edit the grader, enlarge its budget, erase a failure, or grant itself permissions. Those controls stay with the experiment and its operator.

docs.title: Proposal is not promotion
docs.text:
Search may select a best measured artifact. That selection grants no production authority: promotion — actually deploying the selected artifact — is an external governance act that no candidate and no search policy can perform. A run ends with a recommendation and its evidence, never with a deployment. The harness- and policy-evolution examples print this boundary explicitly (promotion=external); see the harness evolution guide.

The authority invariants are canonical in the architecture and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Make a proposer attach a glowing self-assessment to its proposal metadata. Predict metrics identical to the same candidate without the self-praise: metadata is candidate-controlled, measurement is not.

Previous: Trust a shipped contract · Next: Fail with a type, not a zero

docs.title: Budgets and reproducibility
docs.text:
Budget can cap evaluations, proposal trials, reported tokens, and wall time. The seed costs one evaluation and no proposal trial. Each authorized successor costs one trial and, when valid and measured, one evaluation. Components cannot widen their allocation; a run overlay may only narrow the task budget.

Usage is committed with the history. summary() and inspect() aggregate task usage, while experience_usage() reports pushed and pulled memory work on its separate meter. Resource exhaustion remains a typed failure or stop reason, never a low score.

Deterministic callables, canonical artifacts, recorded random seeds, and named random substreams make local logical decisions reproducible. External provider behavior is not made deterministic merely by recording a seed; declare the provider configuration and retain its observations without overstating the guarantee.

See Bound cost for the declaration patterns.

docs.title: Trust a shipped contract
docs.text: You wrote a custom evaluator, codec, or search program. How do you know it obeys the same rules the built-in components obey? You run the same published tests the library runs on itself.

docs.title: What a conformance suite is
docs.text:
meta_evolve.conformance publishes one pytest-native suite per extension component family. Each suite is a plain class of laws whose collaborators arrive as fixtures: subclass it, name the subclass Test... so pytest collects it, override the fixtures with your component, and the laws run against your implementation.

published suite               your test module
───────────────               ────────────────
ArtifactCodecTests      <--   class TestMyCodec(ArtifactCodecTests):
  law: decode(encode(v))          fixture: my codec
  law: decode is validation       fixture: rejected payloads
  law: no aliasing                fixture: mutable values

The suites install through an explicit extra, so using the library never pulls in a test runner:

uv sync --extra conformance

docs.title: What the library proves about itself
docs.text:
Every published suite is subclassed inside the repository's own tests, so the built-in codecs, evaluators, policies, and search programs pass exactly the laws an extension author receives. A suite also states what it does not check as carefully as what it does: EvaluatorTests skips its typed-failure law, visibly, when a subclass declares no rejected candidates, and ArtifactCodecTests does the same for its aliasing law. Silence is never counted as passing.

One law is easy to think redundant and is not: EvaluatorTests checks that scoring does not edit the candidate. With built-in codecs an evaluator only ever sees a frozen decoded value — but a custom codec that returns the instance it was handed gives the evaluator the real thing, so the law waits where the damage would land.

docs.title: When you reach for one
docs.text:
• You registered an artifact domain — run your codec through ArtifactCodecTests, as Add an artifact domain does in its final step.
  • You wrote an evaluator, context policy, workspace, sandbox, search program, or repository proposer — the operations lab lists every family and its published suite.

Suite contents and deliberate limitations are canonical in the extensions guide and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Subclass ArtifactCodecTests around a codec whose decode returns the exact instance it was handed, and declare one mutable value. Predict a named aliasing-law failure, not a vague error: the suite tells you which contract your codec broke.

Previous: Attach evidence to results · Next: Keep authority where it belongs

docs.title: Encode any artifact
docs.text: The loop never inspects what it improves. A number, a prompt, a repository, a harness — every artifact travels as a typed payload that one registered codec translates, so no coordinator code branches on what you evolve.

docs.title: Six built-in kinds
docs.text:
Every artifact is stored under a (kind, representation) key. Six keys ship built in:

Kind Representation What it holds python-value canonical-json any canonically serializable value — the default text utf8-text-v1 one UTF-8 document: a prompt, a config, an essay source-tree utf8-tree-v1 an immutable directory of UTF-8 files skill-set utf8-tree-v1 named skill documents agent-harness harness-v2 planner text and frozen context-policy data search-policy policy-manifest-v1 declarative search-policy values

Support-response optimization and skill evolution run two of these through the identical meta.run call site; SQL migrations registers a seventh, custom domain and is the runnable tour of everything on this page.

docs.title: Kind versus representation
docs.text: The kind, never the bytes, decides which codec reads a committed payload. source-tree and skill-set share the same tree bytes (utf8-tree-v1) and still decode differently, because a payload's meaning is a declared contract rather than an inference from its shape.

docs.title: Why custom domains stay durable-local
docs.text:
A registered custom codec is a live Python object with no verifiable manifest. A durable run must be reopenable by a reader who can decode every payload from the record alone — a payload another machine cannot decode is not shareable evidence. So durable-local mode accepts only the six built-in keys and rejects a custom codec before writing any event, with no silent fallback. A local run with a custom domain still works and may still write durable storage; reopening it later means rebuilding the same registry in Python, which grants decoding, not resumption.

To build a domain end to end, follow Add an artifact domain. Codec laws are canonical in the programming model and the published conformance suite, and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Seed a text task with a tuple instead of a string. Predict a typed refusal at ingress — utf8-text-v1 tasks require a str value — before any trial runs: decode and encode are validation, not best-effort coercion.

Previous: Count the work exactly · Build one: Add an artifact domain

docs.title: Evidence and hidden information
docs.text:
A metric says how a candidate measured. Evidence says what an authorized observer saw while producing that measurement. EvaluationResult attaches evaluator-authored EvidenceDraft values beside metrics; ProposalResult may attach proposer-authored hypotheses. The two authorities never merge.

Evidence is the only supported observation channel. A candidate cannot read hidden tests, future evaluations, evaluator internals, or records a context or experience policy did not authorize. AncestorsOnly can push a bounded bundle into context.bundle; pull access can authorize explicit audited queries.

Evidence used during proposal becomes development feedback, even if it started as evaluator output. Held-out evidence stays unavailable until selection and is measured in a separate run. The support rubric records rubric/v1 evidence; the code-repair command evaluator records its environment and bounded process result.

Pull access, audit accounting, and derived_from edges are covered in Experience and derivation.

docs.title: Typed failures
docs.text:
Valid but poor work receives a score and remains rankable. Work that could not be independently measured receives no invented score.

Meta-Evolve preserves distinct failures for invalid output, proposer failure, evaluator failure, timeout, resource exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure. The response differs by type: fix malformed output, repair a grader, reduce cost, change permissions, or retry infrastructure. A single numeric zero would erase that diagnosis and corrupt ranking.

trials() shows each attempt's state, failure, evidence, and usage. inspect() works even when every evaluation failed. Winner-shaped queries raise NoSuccessfulEvaluation when no successful evaluation has metrics; that exception describes the query, while the recorded trial failures describe why.

The results tutorial demonstrates an entirely unrankable run. The code-repair job distinguishes a rankable exit 1 from a grader-fault exit outside the 0/1 protocol.

docs.title: Identity and lineage
docs.text:
A proposer may produce bytes identical to a value already seen. Meta-Evolve still records a new artifact occurrence because content identity and causal identity answer different questions.

The content digest hashes the canonical encoded value. Equal bytes have the same digest and can share stored payload content. The occurrence id names one appearance at one logical position: its parents, producing trial, observations, and usage. Two equal candidates from two attempts therefore retain distinct occurrence ids.

Search, replay, and experience use occurrence identity so deduplication never erases causality. run.lineage() walks the producing occurrences from the seed to a selected artifact; derived_from separately records authorized experience citations.

Inspect this directly in any run:

for artifact in result.inspect().artifacts:
    print(artifact.id, artifact.digest, artifact.parent_ids)

Identity invariants are canonical in the architecture.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
You will improve one customer-support response. The ticket reports a duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. The seed is polite but gives no concrete refund action; the proposer adds an action and timeline without claiming the refund already happened.

The evaluator is deliberately mechanical. It checks only the order id, a concrete $49 refund action, and the absence of a false completion claim.

Before you run it, here is the whole lifecycle: Meta-Evolve evaluates the seed as a baseline, asks the proposer for one successor, evaluates that successor with the same grader, and selects the higher-scoring measured response. The proposer never sees or changes the evaluator.

docs.title: Complete program
docs.text:
import meta_evolve as meta


SEED = "I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'm looking into it."


def propose(_parent):
    return "I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'll submit a $49 refund today; it should appear in 5–7 business days."


def grade(reply):
    checks = ("#4021" in reply, "$49" in reply and "refund" in reply.lower(), "already refunded" not in reply.lower() and "refund is complete" not in reply.lower())
    return sum(checks) / len(checks)


result = meta.improve(seed=SEED, proposer=propose, evaluator=grade, trials=1)
print(result.best())

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Execution is optional while reading. From a repository checkout, run:

RunResult 
uv run python examples/learn/support_response/quickstart.py

I'm sorry about the duplicate $49 charge for order #4021. I'll submit a $49 refund today; it should appear in 5–7 business days.

docs.title: Read the declaration
docs.text:
improve() receives four job-level inputs:

Input Role in this run seed The initial response and evaluated baseline proposer A callable that creates a possible successor evaluator An independent callable that assigns the three-check score trials The maximum number of proposed successors, excluding the seed

The seed passes two checks: it contains #4021 and makes no false completion claim, but it promises no refund action. Its score is 2/3. The successor passes all three checks, so best() prints it with score 1.0. The output is the selected artifact value, not a deployment or a message sent to a customer.

docs.title: Distinguish poor work from failure
docs.text: A low score is rankable work. A proposer exception, malformed candidate, or grader exception is recorded as a typed, unrankable failure. Those distinctions matter once the grader is external or expensive: zero says “valid work measured poorly,” while a typed failure says no trustworthy score was produced.

docs.title: Change one thing and predict
docs.text:
Set trials=0. The proposer will not run, but the seed will still be evaluated as the baseline and returned by best(). Restore trials=1 before continuing so the next page has both the seed and its successor to inspect.

This page contains one experiment. Next, learn what its run returns.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: You will install Meta-Evolve, verify the import, and know which execution mode you are using. The default path is local, in-memory, and dependency-free.

docs.title: Choose one installation path
docs.text:
For an application that already uses uv, add the released package to that application and verify that Python can import it:

uv add meta-evolve
uv run python -c "import meta_evolve; print(meta_evolve.__version__)"

The second command should print a version and exit successfully. uv add changes the application's dependency declaration; it does not create or run an evolution.

For a Meta-Evolve source checkout, reproduce the repository's locked development environment instead:

uv sync --locked --dev
uv run pytest -q

The test count may change as the project grows, but the command should finish without failures. You do not need the optional browser or a model-provider SDK for the first evolution.

docs.title: What gets installed
docs.text:
No model provider is required. A proposer and evaluator can be ordinary Python callables. Durable storage, a user-owned SDK, and subprocess grading are opt-in edges introduced later.

The default improve() call runs synchronously in the current Python process and stores its history in memory. Closing the process discards that in-memory history; persistence is a separate choice covered later.

docs.title: Installation failures are not evaluation results
docs.text:
If import fails, fix the environment before starting an experiment; an import or installation error is not a poor candidate score. If a later run records a typed failure, inspect the returned run instead of treating it as zero.

Next, run your first evolution.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
You will query a successful run for its winner and history, then diagnose a run where nothing was rankable. A Run is a read-only handle over committed facts; the queries do not rerun the proposer or evaluator.

The support example below performs one experiment declaration twice for a fair comparison, then creates an isolated failure variant solely to show diagnosis. The successful run and the failure-only run are separate histories; creating the diagnostic example cannot contaminate the successful result.

docs.title: Complete results tour
docs.text:
"""Tour every public result-query job with the support-response run."""

from __future__ import annotations

import meta_evolve as meta
from meta_evolve.domain import EvaluatorFailure
from meta_evolve.errors import RunsNotComparable

from rubric import SEED, grade_response, propose_response, support_task, run_support


def all_failures() -> meta.Run:
    def broken_grader(_candidate):
        return EvaluatorFailure(message="judge service unavailable")

    return meta.improve(
        seed=SEED,
        proposer=lambda parent: parent,
        evaluator=broken_grader,
        trials=1,
    )


def incompatible_run() -> meta.Run:
    def changed_grader(candidate):
        return grade_response(candidate)

    task = support_task()
    changed_task = meta.Task(
        evaluator=changed_grader,
        objectives=task.objectives,
        budget=task.budget,
    )
    return meta.run(
        meta.Experiment(
            task=changed_task,
            seed=SEED,
            proposer=propose_response,
            search=meta.Greedy(max_trials=2),
        )
    )


def main() -> None:
    result = run_support(random_seed=0)
    second = run_support(random_seed=1)
    winner = result.best()
    trial = result.best_trial()
    print(f"best={winner.value}")
    print(f"best_trial={trial.logical_step}:{trial.metrics['overall']:.2f}")
    print(f"lineage={[item.logical_step for item in result.lineage(winner)]}")
    print(f"trials={[item.state for item in result.trials()]}")
    print(f"summary={result.summary().primary_score:.2f}")
    overview = result.inspect().overview
    print(f"inspect={overview.lifecycle}/{overview.rankability}")
    print(f"compare_tied={result.compare(second).tied}")
    try:
        result.compare(incompatible_run())
    except RunsNotComparable:
        print("compare_refusal=changed evaluator")

    failed = all_failures()
    try:
        failed.best()
    except meta.NoSuccessfulEvaluation:
        failures = [type(item.failure).__name__ for item in failed.inspect().trials]
        print(f"all_failure_diagnosis={failures}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
